implementation_notes: Scala makes laziness a language feature: `lazy val config = Config.load()` is compiled to a thread-safe state machine over volatile fields - Scala 3 implements SIP-20 v6, where a state word moves from uninitialised through 'being initialised' and 'concurrently read' to initialised, so exactly one thread runs the initialiser and other readers either wait or observe the published value - and `object` initialization is performed once under the JVM's class-initialisation lock. Nothing in the source shows the double check; the classic structure survives only as the explanation of what the compiler emits. A hand-written volatile-plus-synchronized accessor is justified only where the value must be invalidated and rebuilt (lazy val cannot be reset) or where the generated guard's cost is measurable in a very hot per-instance path.
pitfalls: A lazy val cannot be reset: invalidation needs an AtomicReference or a var with an explicit lock, and a recursive lazy val has undefined behaviour (the Scala 3 reference notes it may deadlock).
The initialiser runs on the first accessing thread, so a slow build delays every other thread that needs the same val - and any exception it throws surfaces at an unrelated call site.

A lazy val referenced during construction of its own object can re-enter the constructor (the classic 'lazy val during initialisation' hazard), so the initialiser must not depend on the partially built instance.
Serialisation and reflection read fields directly, bypassing the lazy guard, which can publish nulls for a value that was never forced.
